claim: Posterior parietal cortex (PPC) has been implicated in navigation.
source: Posterior parietal cortex (PPC) has been implicated in navigation, in the control of movement, and in visually-guided decisions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established view in the literature.

claim: Posterior parietal cortex (PPC) has been implicated in the control of movement.
source: Posterior parietal cortex (PPC) has been implicated in navigation, in the control of movement, and in visually-guided decisions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established view in the literature.

claim: Posterior parietal cortex (PPC) has been implicated in visually-guided decisions.
source: Posterior parietal cortex (PPC) has been implicated in navigation, in the control of movement, and in visually-guided decisions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established view in the literature.

claim: PPC neurons were selective for specific combinations of the animal's spatial position and heading angle.
source: PPC neurons were selective for specific combinations of the animal's spatial position and heading angle.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The selectivity for position and heading closely predicted the activity of individual PPC neurons.
source: This selectivity closely predicted both the activity of individual PPC neurons, and the arrangement of their collective firing patterns in choice-selective sequences.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results and correlation analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The selectivity for position and heading closely predicted the arrangement of collective firing patterns in choice-selective sequences.
source: This selectivity closely predicted both the activity of individual PPC neurons, and the arrangement of their collective firing patterns in choice-selective sequences.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Choice-selective sequences reflected PPC encoding of the animal's navigation trajectory.
source: These sequences reflected PPC encoding of the animal's navigation trajectory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the modeling results.

claim: Using decision as a predictor instead of heading yielded worse fits.
source: Using decision as a predictor instead of heading yielded worse fits, and using it in addition to heading only slightly improved the fits.
evidence: This is supported by the model comparison results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Using decision in addition to heading only slightly improved the fits.
source: Using decision as a predictor instead of heading yielded worse fits, and using it in addition to heading only slightly improved the fits.
evidence: This is supported by the model comparison results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Alternative models based on visual or motor variables were inferior.
source: Alternative models based on visual or motor variables were inferior.
evidence: This is supported by the playback experiment and motor model comparison.

claim: When mice use vision to choose their trajectories, a large fraction of parietal cortex activity can be predicted from simple attributes such as spatial position and heading.
source: We conclude that when mice use vision to choose their trajectories, a large fraction of parietal cortex activity can be predicted from simple attributes such as spatial position and heading.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data and modeling results.

claim: PPC is recognized as a key nexus of sensorimotor integration.
source: Posterior parietal cortex (PPC) is recognized as a key nexus of sensorimotor integration (Milner and Goodale, 2006), and the large literature concerning its functions has led to disparate views as to its role.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurons in monkey PPC can be influenced by movements of eyes, head, limbs, and body.
source: For instance, neurons in monkey PPC can be influenced by movements of eyes, head, limbs, and body (Cohen and Andersen, 2002), by the intention to execute such movements (Andersen and Buneo, 2002), or by the attention devoted to the resulting position (Bisley and Goldberg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurons in monkey PPC can be influenced by the intention to execute movements.
source: For instance, neurons in monkey PPC can be influenced by movements of eyes, head, limbs, and body (Cohen and Andersen, 2002), by the intention to execute such movements (Andersen and Buneo, 2002), or by the attention devoted to the resulting position (Bisley and Goldberg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurons in monkey PPC can be influenced by the attention devoted to the resulting position.
source: For instance, neurons in monkey PPC can be influenced by movements of eyes, head, limbs, and body (Cohen and Andersen, 2002), by the intention to execute such movements (Andersen and Buneo, 2002), or by the attention devoted to the resulting position (Bisley and Goldberg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurons in rat PPC can encode attributes of body posture.
source: Neurons in rat PPC, moreover, can encode attributes of body posture (Mimica et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PPC has a role in decision making, especially for decisions based on vision.
source: Another set of experiments indicates a role of PPC in decision making, especially for decisions based on vision (Andersen and Cui, 2009; Erlich et al., 2015; Goard et al., 2016; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Katz et al., 2016; Latimer et al., 2015; Licata et al., 2017; Platt and Glimcher, 1999; Raposo et al., 2014; Sugrue et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Decision signals are widespread in rodent PPC populations, where they are mixed with other signals.
source: Studies in rodents found decision signals to be widespread in PPC populations, where they are mixed with other signals (Goard et al., 2016; Pho et al., 2018; Raposo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Memory-based decision signals are remarkably common in PPC, with each PPC neuron firing only for a particular decision and only at a particular moment in a stereotyped sequence.
source: One study, in particular, probed memory-based decision signals and found them to be remarkably common, with each PPC neuron firing only for a particular decision and only at a particular moment in a stereotyped sequence (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: PPC has an important role in spatial navigation in rodents.
source: A third set of studies, performed in rodents, suggested an important role of PPC in spatial navigation (McNaughton et al., 1994; Nitz, 2006; Nitz, 2012; Save and Poucet, 2000; Save and Poucet, 2009; Whitlock et al., 2012; Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Neurons in rat PPC encode combinations of spatial location and body movement.
source: Neurons in rat PPC encode combinations of spatial location and body movement (McNaughton et al., 1994; Nitz, 2006; Nitz, 2012; Whitlock et al., 2012; Wilber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Inactivating rat PPC can impair navigation.
source: Inactivating it, moreover, can impair navigation (Save and Poucet, 2000; Save and Poucet, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Neuronal populations may benefit from a strategy of 'mixed selectivity', where neurons are tuned to mixtures of task-related variables.
source: Neuronal populations may benefit from a strategy of 'mixed selectivity', where neurons are tuned to mixtures of task-related variables (Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mixed selectivity has been observed in PPC neurons of monkeys.
source: Mixed selectivity has been observed in PPC neurons of both monkeys (Freedman and Assad, 2009; Park et al., 2014; Rishel et al., 2013) and rats (Raposo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mixed selectivity has been observed in PPC neurons of rats.
source: Mixed selectivity has been observed in PPC neurons of both monkeys (Freedman and Assad, 2009; Park et al., 2014; Rishel et al., 2013) and rats (Raposo et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mice performed a visual two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) contrast-detection task by walking on an air-suspended ball through a virtual corridor.
source: Head-fixed mice performed a visual two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) contrast-detection task by walking on an air-suspended ball (Dombeck et al., 2010) through a virtual corridor (Figure 1a, Video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and task design.

claim: One of the corridor's side walls, chosen randomly, contained a vertical grating.
source: One of the corridor's side walls, chosen randomly, contained a vertical grating, and mice indicated that side by turning into the left or right arms at the end of the corridor (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: Mice indicated the side with the grating by turning into the left or right arms at the end of the corridor.
source: One of the corridor's side walls, chosen randomly, contained a vertical grating, and mice indicated that side by turning into the left or right arms at the end of the corridor (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: Successful trials were followed by a water reward.
source: Successful trials were followed by a water reward, and unsuccessful ones by a brief white-noise sound.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: Unsuccessful trials were followed by a brief white-noise sound.
source: Successful trials were followed by a water reward, and unsuccessful ones by a brief white-noise sound.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: The grating's contrast was varied randomly across trials to control task difficulty.
source: To control the task difficulty, we varied the grating's contrast randomly across trials.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: Contrast exerted a powerful influence on performance: mice frequently chose the correct side for high-contrast stimuli, and performed at chance when contrast was low or zero.
source: Accordingly, contrast exerted a powerful influence on performance: mice frequently chose the correct side for high-contrast stimuli, and performed at chance when contrast was low or zero (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by the psychometric curve data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Visual decisions strongly influenced navigation throughout the corridor, as mice typically turned towards the intended side before reaching the end.
source: These visual decisions strongly influenced navigation throughout the corridor, as mice typically turned towards the intended side before reaching the end (Figure 1d–h).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory data shown in Figure 1d-h.

claim: The paths that ended in left and right choices progressively deviated from each other as the animal started heading towards the chosen side before reaching the end of the corridor.
source: In these coordinates, the paths that ended in left and right choices progressively deviated from each other: the animal started heading towards the chosen side before reaching the end of the corridor.
evidence: This is supported by trajectory data shown in Figure 1d-f.

claim: The dependence of heading angle on decision was particularly clear for trials with higher contrast, which were easier.
source: This dependence of heading angle θ on decision was particularly clear for trials with higher contrast, which were easier (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The final choice could be predicted from the heading angle with increasing accuracy as the mouse reached the end of the corridor.
source: The final choice could thus be predicted from the heading angle with increasing accuracy as the mouse reached the end of the corridor (Figure 1g,h).
evidence: This is supported by the predictability analysis shown in Figure 1g,h.

claim: PPC population activity was measured using 2-photon calcium imaging.
source: While mice performed this task, we measured PPC population activity using 2-photon calcium imaging (Figure 1i,j).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Retinotopic maps were obtained using widefield imaging to identify the borders of visual cortical areas.
source: To identify the borders of visual cortical areas we obtained retinotopic maps using widefield imaging (Figure 1i), and identified PPC as a region anterior to the V1 region, along a contour of pixels that represent a retinotopic azimuth of 60–80 degrees.
evidence: This describes the experimental method for identifying PPC.

claim: PPC was identified as a region anterior to the V1 region, along a contour of pixels that represent a retinotopic azimuth of 60–80 degrees.
source: To identify the borders of visual cortical areas we obtained retinotopic maps using widefield imaging (Figure 1i), and identified PPC as a region anterior to the V1 region, along a contour of pixels that represent a retinotopic azimuth of 60–80 degrees.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying PPC.

claim: The average stereotaxic coordinates of PPC were close to the coordinates used in previous studies of mouse PPC (2.0 mm posterior, 1.7 mm lateral).
source: The average stereotaxic coordinates of this region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) were close to the coordinates used in previous studies of mouse PPC (2.0 mm posterior, 1.7 mm lateral, Goard et al., 2016; Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior studies and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Suite2p image-processing pipeline was applied to obtain calcium traces from well-identified cell bodies.
source: To obtain calcium traces from well-identified cell bodies we applied Suite2p, an image-processing pipeline that provides image registration, cell detection, and neuropil correction, followed by manual curation (Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: All recorded PPC cells could be divided into two groups forming distinct, choice-dependent sequences of activation.
source: In agreement with previous observations made in a memory-based task (Harvey et al., 2012), all the recorded PPC cells could be divided into two groups forming distinct, choice-dependent sequences of activation (Figure 1k–n).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1k-n and agrees with prior observations.

claim: One group of cells responded primarily during trials that ended in a leftward choice.
source: One group of cells responded primarily during trials that ended in a leftward choice (Figure 1k,l), and the other during trials that ended in a rightward choice (Figure 1m,n).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1k,l.

claim: One group of cells responded primarily during trials that ended in a rightward choice.
source: One group of cells responded primarily during trials that ended in a leftward choice (Figure 1k,l), and the other during trials that ended in a rightward choice (Figure 1m,n).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1m,n.

claim: Cells could be ordered so that the responses of each group of cells could be arranged in a sequence of activations.
source: Moreover, cells could be ordered so that the responses of each group of cells could be arranged in a sequence of activations (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1k-n and agrees with prior observations.

claim: Some cells that responded during the initial part of the task tended to fire in both trials that ended with left and right choices.
source: While some cells that responded during the initial part of the task tended to fire in both trials that ended with left and right choices, the rest of the cells unambiguously fired only in one or the other of those trials.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1k-n.

claim: Most cells unambiguously fired only in trials ending with one choice or the other.
source: While some cells that responded during the initial part of the task tended to fire in both trials that ended with left and right choices, the rest of the cells unambiguously fired only in one or the other of those trials.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1k-n.

claim: An example neuron tended to respond in precise combinations of position z (~60 cm into the corridor) and heading angle θ (~20 deg to the right).
source: Plotting the neuron's activity on top of the individual trajectories reveals that the neuron tended to respond in precise combinations of position z (~60 cm into the corridor) and heading angle θ (~20 deg to the right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a,b for an example neuron.

claim: The example neuron was active whenever a trajectory brought the mouse to the appropriate combinations of position and heading, regardless of final choice.
source: The neuron was active whenever a trajectory brought the mouse to the appropriate combinations of position and heading, regardless of final choice.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2a,b.

claim: A simple 'position-heading field' was sufficient to accurately predict the calcium activity of the example neuron.
source: Indeed, a simple 'position-heading field' was sufficient to accurately predict the calcium activity of the neuron (Figure 2c–g).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2c-g.

claim: The position-heading field correctly predicted the occasional trials when the neuron responded during leftward choices.
source: For instance, the position-heading field correctly predicted the occasional trials when the neuron responded during leftward choices (above the black bar in Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Position-heading fields provided a good account of the activity across the population.
source: Position-heading fields provided a good account of the activity across the population (Figure 2h–j).
evidence: This is demonstrated with multiple example cells in Figure 2h-j.

claim: The median correlation between model predictions and calcium traces was 27% (±16% m.a.d., n = 7,646 cells) when pooling across seven mice.
source: The median correlation between model predictions and calcium traces was 27% (±16% m.a.d., n = 7,646 cells) when pooling across seven mice, and ranged from 19% to 41% in individual mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the model performance across the population.

claim: The median correlation between model predictions and calcium traces ranged from 19% to 41% in individual mice.
source: The median correlation between model predictions and calcium traces was 27% (±16% m.a.d., n = 7,646 cells) when pooling across seven mice, and ranged from 19% to 41% in individual mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the model performance across individual mice.

claim: The correlation values are high, given that all measures were cross-validated.
source: These values are high, given that all measures were cross-validated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model performance results.

claim: Position-heading fields were largely sufficient to explain the arrangement of parietal cortex responses in choice-dependent sequences.
source: Position-heading fields were also largely sufficient to explain the arrangement of parietal cortex responses in choice-dependent sequences (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The position-heading model predictions produce orderly, choice-dependent sequences of activation, replicating the essential features of those seen in the data.
source: The resulting predictions produce orderly, choice-dependent sequences of activation, replicating the essential features of those seen in the data (Figure 1k–n).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 3 with Figure 1k-n.

claim: Choice-dependent sequences of activation emerge from a combination of two factors: the fact that mice take different trajectories in trials that end with leftward vs. rightward choices, and the fact that different cells prefer different combinations of position and heading.
source: These choice-dependent sequences of activation emerge from a combination of two factors: the fact that mice take different trajectories in trials that end with leftward vs. rightward choices (Figure 1d–f), and the fact that different cells prefer different combinations of position and heading (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figures 1d-f and 3c,d.

claim: Cells that responded preferentially in trials ending in leftward choices almost invariably preferred negative (leftward) heading values.
source: Almost invariably, the former preferred negative (leftward) heading angles, and the latter preferred positive (rightward) heading angles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Cells that responded preferentially in trials ending in rightward choices almost invariably preferred positive (rightward) heading values.
source: Almost invariably, the former preferred negative (leftward) heading angles, and the latter preferred positive (rightward) heading angles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The preferred heading of PPC cells was sufficient to explain their selectivity for choice.
source: The preferred heading of these PPC cells was thus sufficient to explain their selectivity for choice: cells with preferred leftward heading were more likely to fire when the animal headed leftward, which occurred most often when the animal ultimately chose the left arm.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A model f(z, d) where responses depend on position and decision alone is implicit in representations where neurons are arranged in choice-selective activation sequences.
source: A model f(z, d) where responses depend on position and decision alone is implicit in representations where neurons are arranged in choice-selective activation sequences (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a reference to the interpretation of prior work.

claim: The position-decision model provided only a rough approximation of the trial-by-trial activity of individual cells, missing its graded dependence on heading angle θ.
source: However, it provided only a rough approximation of the trial-by-trial activity of individual cells, missing its graded dependence on heading angle θ (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The position-heading model had correlations higher by 5.6% than for the position-decision model (±9.8%, m.a.d., n = 7646 neurons).
source: This analysis gave a clear advantage to the position-heading model, with correlations higher by 5.6% than for the position-decision model (±9.8%, m.a.d., n = 7646 neurons, Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The advantage of the position-heading model over the position-decision model was visible in individual sessions.
source: This advantage was visible also in individual sessions (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c.

claim: A model with all three predictors (position, heading, and decision) performed only slightly better than the model with position and heading alone.
source: Furthermore, a model with all three predictors performed only slightly better than the model with position and heading alone (Figure 4d–f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: The extended model f(z, θ, d) improved the correlations by only 0.4% (±2.9%, m.a.d., n = 7646 neurons) compared to the simple position-heading model.
source: Across all neurons, the extended model performed at a similar cross-validated level as the simple position-heading model, improving the correlations by only 0.4% (±2.9%, m.a.d., n = 7646 neurons, Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Adding heading angle θ to a model that already includes decision d considerably improved the fits, with a median increase in correlation of 6.1% (±6.1% m.a.d., n = 7646 neurons).
source: Conversely, adding heading angle θ to a model that already includes d considerably improved the fits, with a median increase in correlation of 6.1% (±6.1% m.a.d., n = 7646 neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance.

claim: Heading angle was a much better predictor of responses than decision.
source: Therefore, heading angle was a much better predictor of responses than decision.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: Much of the activity of PPC neurons in the task can be explained by two spatial attributes: position and heading.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that much of the activity of PPC neurons in our task can be explained by two spatial attributes: position and heading.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: In the experiment, spatial attributes may covary with visual and motor factors.
source: A possible caveat in this conclusion, however, is that in our experiment those spatial attributes may covary with visual and motor factors.
evidence: This is a consideration of potential confounds.

claim: Position and heading determined the visual scene.
source: Position and heading determined the visual scene, and the visual scene could in turn determine the activity of PPC neurons, especially given that mouse PPC overlaps at least partially with regions of higher visual cortex (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Zhuang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the task structure, supported by citations.

claim: Mouse PPC overlaps at least partially with regions of higher visual cortex.
source: Position and heading determined the visual scene, and the visual scene could in turn determine the activity of PPC neurons, especially given that mouse PPC overlaps at least partially with regions of higher visual cortex (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Zhuang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Position in z-θ space is determined by the animal's movement on the ball and therefore by motor factors such as linear and angular velocity.
source: Likewise, position in z-θ space is itself determined by the animal's movement on the ball and therefore by motor factors such as linear and angular velocity, which may in turn determine PPC activity (McNaughton et al., 1994; Nitz, 2006; Whitlock, 2014; Whitlock et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the task structure, supported by citations.

claim: In the playback condition only a minority of PPC neurons maintained their preferences for position and heading, and even in those neurons the responses were much weaker.
source: In this playback condition only a minority of PPC neurons maintained their preferences for position and heading, and even in those neurons the responses were much weaker (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: For the majority of PPC cells, activity in the playback condition was not predictable from the preferences for position and heading estimated during the task.
source: Moreover, for the majority of PPC cells, activity in the playback condition was not predictable from the preferences for position and heading estimated during the task.
evidence: This is an observation from the playback experiment.

claim: Parietal areas of the mouse cortex are considered to overlap with visual areas RL, A, and AM.
source: This is perhaps remarkable, given that parietal areas of the mouse cortex are considered to overlap with visual areas RL, A, and AM (Hovde et al., 2018; Kirkcaldie, 2012), which contain retinotopic visual representations (Garrett et al., 2014; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Visual areas RL, A, and AM contain retinotopic visual representations.
source: This is perhaps remarkable, given that parietal areas of the mouse cortex are considered to overlap with visual areas RL, A, and AM (Hovde et al., 2018; Kirkcaldie, 2012), which contain retinotopic visual representations (Garrett et al., 2014; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Responses measured in primary visual cortex (V1) during the task and during playback were in better agreement than PPC responses.
source: By comparison, responses measured in primary visual cortex (V1) during the task and during playback were in better agreement (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The model based on motor factors performed markedly worse than the model based on position and heading in virtual reality.
source: The model based on motor factors performed markedly worse than the model based on position and heading in virtual reality (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: A Bayesian decoder successfully predicted the position of the animal in position-heading space at individual time points.
source: The decoder successfully predicted the position of the animal in position-heading space at individual time points (Figure 5a) and replicated the animal's trajectory (Figure 5b; Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A Bayesian decoder replicated the animal's trajectory.
source: The decoder successfully predicted the position of the animal in position-heading space at individual time points (Figure 5a) and replicated the animal's trajectory (Figure 5b; Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b and Video 2.

claim: In predicting the final choice, the population decoder was just as good as the animal's actual heading.
source: In predicting the final choice, in fact, the population decoder was just as good as the animal's actual heading: both showed a similar dependence on position z (Figure 5c) and stimulus contrast (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: During visually-guided navigation, populations of PPC neurons encode spatial position and heading angle.
source: This result provides further support for the view that during visually-guided navigation, populations of PPC neurons encode spatial position and heading angle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding results.

claim: The results resonate with the view that rodent PPC encodes combinations of spatial attributes.
source: These results resonate with the view that rodent PPC encodes combinations of spatial attributes (McNaughton et al., 1994; Nitz, 2006; Nitz, 2012; Save and Poucet, 2000; Save and Poucet, 2009; Whitlock et al., 2012; Wilber et al., 2014), but are also fully consistent with the observation that PPC cells can be divided into groups forming distinct sequences of activations depending on upcoming choice (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: The results are fully consistent with the observation that PPC cells can be divided into groups forming distinct sequences of activations depending on upcoming choice.
source: These results resonate with the view that rodent PPC encodes combinations of spatial attributes (McNaughton et al., 1994; Nitz, 2006; Nitz, 2012; Save and Poucet, 2000; Save and Poucet, 2009; Whitlock et al., 2012; Wilber et al., 2014), but are also fully consistent with the observation that PPC cells can be divided into groups forming distinct sequences of activations depending on upcoming choice (Harvey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature, supported by citation.

claim: The division into choice-dependent sequences, and the sequences themselves, could be explained by the effect on PPC of two measurable factors: the trajectories taken by the mouse in different trials, and the preferences of different cells for different combinations of position and heading.
source: However, in our data, this division into choice-dependent sequences, and indeed the sequences themselves, could be explained by the effect on PPC of two measurable factors: the trajectories taken by the mouse in different trials, and the preferences of different cells for different combinations of position and heading.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The selectivity of PPC cells for heading and position explained the cells' apparent selectivity for the mouse's decision.
source: The selectivity of PPC cells for heading and position explained the cells' apparent selectivity for the mouse's decision.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The discrepancy with Harvey et al. (2012) may be due to a difference between the tasks.
source: Perhaps this discrepancy is due to a difference between the tasks: for example in our task, unlike the main task by Harvey et al, the spatial cues indicating the appropriate decision were visible until the end of the corridor.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of differences between studies.

claim: Task differences might have caused the animals to employ different strategies, resulting in genuinely different types of PPC coding across the two tasks.
source: This might have caused the animals to employ different strategies, resulting in genuinely different types of PPC coding across the two tasks.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of differences between studies.

claim: The same combination of spatial factors may also have contributed to the results of Harvey et al. (2012).
source: It is also possible, however, that the same combination of spatial factors also contributed to the results of Harvey et al. (2012).
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of prior work.

claim: The animals' trajectories in Harvey et al. (2012) did exhibit differences in heading angle that correlated with the final decision.
source: Indeed, the animals' trajectories in that study did exhibit differences in heading angle that correlated with the final decision, but trials showing such differences were progressively excluded from analysis until the difference in mean heading angle no longer reached statistical significance.
evidence: This is an observation about the methods used in a prior study.

claim: In Harvey et al. (2012), trials showing differences in heading angle were progressively excluded from analysis until the difference in mean heading angle no longer reached statistical significance.
source: Indeed, the animals' trajectories in that study did exhibit differences in heading angle that correlated with the final decision, but trials showing such differences were progressively excluded from analysis until the difference in mean heading angle no longer reached statistical significance.
evidence: This is an observation about the methods used in a prior study.

claim: The activity of neurons in PPC during a task involving movement, vision, decision, and navigation, can be accurately predicted based on the selectivity of the neurons for two spatial variables: the position of the mouse along the corridor, and its heading angle.
source: In conclusion, we found that the activity of neurons in PPC during a task involving movement, vision, decision, and navigation, can be accurately predicted based on the selectivity of the neurons for two spatial variables: the position of the mouse along the corridor, and its heading angle.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Consideration of selectivity for position and heading, and the mouse's trajectories through virtual space, fully accounts for the apparent formation of decision-dependent activity sequences in this task.
source: Consideration of this selectivity, and the mouse's trajectories through virtual space, fully accounts for the apparent formation of decision-dependent activity sequences in this task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: When mice use vision to guide navigation, parietal cortex encodes navigational attributes such as position and heading rather than visual signals or abstract decisions.
source: In other words, when mice use vision to guide navigation, parietal cortex encodes navigational attributes such as position and heading rather than visual signals or abstract decisions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The results do not completely rule out a possible role of decision signals in shaping the responses of PPC neurons.
source: Our results, however, do not completely rule out a possible role of decision signals in shaping the responses of PPC neurons.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the results.

claim: Adding decision as an explicit variable barely improved the fits of the position-heading model, but did not make them worse as it could have, given that the model fits were cross-validated.
source: We found that adding decision as an explicit variable barely improved the fits of the position-heading model, but did not make them worse as it could have, given that the model fits were cross-validated.
evidence: This is an observation from the model comparison results.

claim: The task cannot fully distinguish encoding of navigation variables and of decisions, because trajectory signals might strongly covary with an evolving decision variable.
source: Our task, in fact, cannot fully distinguish encoding of navigation variables and of decisions, because trajectory signals might strongly covary with an evolving decision variable.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: An evolving decision variable might be seen not only in covert neural signals, but also in ongoing body movements.
source: Such an evolving decision variable might be seen not only in covert neural signals, but also in ongoing body movements (Dotan et al., 2018; Resulaj et al., 2009; Song and Nakayama, 2009; Spivey et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The clear dependence of trajectories on stimulus contrast is consistent with a close relationship between a decision variable and the animal's trajectories.
source: In our task, the clear dependence of trajectories on stimulus contrast is consistent with a close relationship between a decision variable and the animal's trajectories.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: It may not be possible to distinguish the neural encoding of navigation variables and decision variables.
source: It may not be possible to distinguish the neural encoding of the two.
evidence: This is a limitation of the experimental approach.

claim: PPC activity could be influenced by a multitude of postural attributes that were not monitored, and some of these may correlate with the apparent decision signals that improved the fits.
source: Moreover, PPC activity could be influenced by a multitude of postural attributes that we did not monitor, and some of these may correlate with the apparent decision signals that improved our fits.
evidence: This is speculation about unmeasured variables.

claim: There is mounting evidence that postural and other motor variables act as powerful determinants of activity throughout the cortex.
source: Indeed, there is mounting evidence that postural and other motor variables act as powerful determinants of activity throughout the cortex (Musall et al., 2018; Stringer et al., 2018) including PPC (Mimica et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Neurons in PPC may be sensitive to postural variables that in turn predict heading.
source: The same observation, in fact, can be made for the apparent selectivity of PPC neurons for heading: perhaps neurons in PPC are sensitive to postural variables that in turn predict heading.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative interpretations.

claim: The precise motor, postural, or cognitive correlates of heading and decision need further examination, ideally with tasks explicitly designed to distinguish these correlates.
source: The precise motor, postural, or cognitive correlates of heading and decision need further examination, ideally with tasks explicitly designed to distinguish these correlates.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: The activity of large populations of PPC neurons can be explained based on simple embodied quantities such as heading and position in the environment.
source: In the meantime, our results indicate that the activity of large populations of PPC neurons can be explained based on simple embodied quantities such as heading and position in the environment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Seven mice were used in the experiments (two C57bl/6 mice, three Camk2a-tTA;Ai93(TITL-GCaMP6f);Emx1-IRES-Cre mice, and two Ai95(RCL-GCaMP6f)-D; Slc17a7-IRES2-Cre-D).
source: We report here on experiments performed in seven mice (two C57bl/6 mice, three Camk2a-tTA;Ai93(TITL-GCaMP6f);Emx1-IRES-Cre mice, and two Ai95(RCL-GCaMP6f)-D; Slc17a7-IRES2-Cre-D), of both sexes, aged 80–241 days during imaging sessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: The mice were of both sexes, aged 80–241 days during imaging sessions.
source: We report here on experiments performed in seven mice (two C57bl/6 mice, three Camk2a-tTA;Ai93(TITL-GCaMP6f);Emx1-IRES-Cre mice, and two Ai95(RCL-GCaMP6f)-D; Slc17a7-IRES2-Cre-D), of both sexes, aged 80–241 days during imaging sessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: The Ai93-Emx1 strain tends to show epileptiform activity.
source: The recordings from the three Ai93-Emx1 mice were made before we realized that this strain tends to show epileptiform activity (Steinmetz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The recordings from Ai93-Emx1 mice were tested for epileptiform activity and the results were negative.
source: We tested our recordings for this activity and the results were negative.
evidence: This describes a control analysis performed.

claim: Epileptiform activity can be missed in posterior regions of the cortex.
source: However, we only imaged posterior regions of the cortex, where epileptiform activity can be missed (Steinmetz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mouse-by-mouse analysis did not reveal differences between the strains used.
source: For this reason, we recorded from the other strains and we ran a mouse-by-mouse analysis. This analysis did not reveal differences between the strains we used (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), so we pooled the data across all of them.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The virtual reality environment consisted of a 110 cm long T-Maze with a 20 cm wide corridor.
source: The virtual reality environment consisted of a 110 cm long T-Maze with a 20 cm wide corridor.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Virtual position was never allowed to be less than 5 cm to any wall.
source: Virtual position was never allowed to be less than 5 cm to any wall.
evidence: This describes a constraint in the virtual environment.

claim: The grating was superimposed on a noise texture (20% visual contrast), which was identical on both walls and across trials.
source: The grating was superimposed on a noise texture (20% visual contrast), which was identical on both walls and across trials.
evidence: This describes the visual stimulus design.

claim: The spatial frequency of the grating was 14 cycles/m.
source: The spatial frequency of the grating was 14 cycles/m, and the resulting spatial frequency in the mouse visual field (in cycles/deg) varied depending on the distance and angle of the wall relative to the mouse.
evidence: This describes the visual stimulus design.

claim: A 40% visual contrast noise pattern was applied to the floor of the corridor (and the ceiling, in some experiments).
source: To provide additional visual flow and context, a 40% visual contrast noise pattern was applied to the floor of the corridor (and the ceiling, in some experiments).
evidence: This describes the visual stimulus design.

claim: Trials ending in a wrong choice were repeated until finished correctly to prevent the animal from developing behavioral biases.
source: However, to prevent the animal from developing behavioral biases, trials ending in a wrong choice were repeated until finished correctly, at which point the next trial in the sequence was again a random trial.
evidence: This describes the behavioral training protocol.

claim: Correct trials were indicated by a brief beep (0.1 s, 6.6 kHz) tone.
source: Correct trials were indicated by a brief beep (0.1 s, 6.6 kHz) tone, while error trials were indicated by a brief (0.2 s) white noise sound.
evidence: This describes the feedback provided to the animal.

claim: Error trials were indicated by a brief (0.2 s) white noise sound.
source: Correct trials were indicated by a brief beep (0.1 s, 6.6 kHz) tone, while error trials were indicated by a brief (0.2 s) white noise sound.
evidence: This describes the feedback provided to the animal.

claim: Trials not finished within 45 s were timed out and a longer (3 s) white-noise sound was played.
source: Trials not finished within 45 s were timed out and a longer (3 s) white-noise sound was played.
evidence: This describes the task protocol.

claim: Mice typically performed between 200 and 400 trials per session (session duration 45–60 min).
source: Mice typically performed between 200 and 400 trials per session (session duration 45–60 min), with typical duration of the finished trials of 6.0 ± 2.0 (median ±m.a.d.) seconds, varying between 4.7 and 11.6 s (median values) for individual animals.
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance.

claim: The typical duration of finished trials was 6.0 ± 2.0 (median ±m.a.d.) seconds, varying between 4.7 and 11.6 s (median values) for individual animals.
source: Mice typically performed between 200 and 400 trials per session (session duration 45–60 min), with typical duration of the finished trials of 6.0 ± 2.0 (median ±m.a.d.) seconds, varying between 4.7 and 11.6 s (median values) for individual animals.
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance.

claim: Mice required different numbers of training sessions to reach behavioral performance sufficient to be considered for imaging (7 to 36 sessions, 21 on average across seven animals).
source: Mice required different numbers of training sessions to reach behavioral performance sufficient to be considered for imaging (7 to 36 sessions, 21 on average across seven animals).
evidence: This describes the training protocol.

claim: Two-photon imaging was performed using a standard resonant B-Scope microscope equipped with Nikon 16x, 0.8 NA objective.
source: Two-photon imaging (total of 33 recording sessions) was performed using a standard resonant B-Scope microscope (ThorLabs Inc.) equipped with Nikon 16x, 0.8 NA objective, and controlled by ScanImage 4.2 (Pologruto et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the imaging method.

claim: Frame rate was set to ~30 Hz, with the field of view of ~500×500 µm (512 × 512 pixels).
source: Frame rate was set to ~30 Hz, with the field of view of ~500×500 µm (512 × 512 pixels).
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.

claim: The frame rate was shared between 3–5 imaging planes spanning the depth of L2/3 using a piezo focusing device, resulting in a 6–10 Hz effective sampling rate per cell.
source: This frame rate was further shared between 3–5 imaging planes spanning the depth of L2/3 using a piezo focusing device (P-725.4CA PIFOC, Physik Instrumente) resulting in a 6–10 Hz effective sampling rate per cell.
evidence: This describes the imaging method.

claim: Excitation light at 970 nm was delivered by an Ultra II femtosecond laser.
source: Excitation light at 970 nm was delivered by an Ultra II femtosecond laser (Coherent, UK)
evidence: This describes the imaging equipment.
